Handmade cloning: recent advances, potential and pitfalls
records.venue: Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology/Journal of animal science and biotechnology
records.abstract: Handmade cloning (HMC) is the most awaited, simple and micromanipulator-free version of somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT). The requirement of expensive micromanipulators and skilled expertise is eliminated in this technique, proving it as a major revolution in the field of embryology. During the past years, many modifications have been incorporated in this technique to boost its efficiency. This alternative approach to micromanipulator based traditional cloning (TC) works wonder in generating comparable or even higher birth rates in addition to declining costs drastically and enabling cryopreservation. This technique is not only applicable to intraspecies nuclear transfer but also to interspecies nuclear transfer (iSCNT) thus permitting conservation of endangered species. It also offers unique possibilities for automation of SCNT which aims at production of transgenic animals that can cure certain human diseases by producing therapeutics hence, providing a healthier future for the wellbeing of humans. The present review aims at highlighting certain aspects of HMC including recent advancements in procedure and factors involved in elevating its efficiency besides covering the potentials and pitfalls of this technique.

Trade and Gendered Labor Outcomes: Evidence from Changing Export Demand in Indonesia
records.abstract: Gender equality in the Indonesian labor market remains a significant concern. According to the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, the disparity between male and female labor force participation (FLFP) has averaged around 30 percentage points over the past decades. Additionally, regarding the wage gap, women earn approximately 30% less than men, irrespective of whether they are in paid employment or self-employment (Sohn, 2015). This economic gender disparity is inefficient and requires attention. The prevailing narrative in the trade policies of many developing countries, including Indonesia, has been centered since the early 1980s on the belief that trade gains primarily stem from export activities. The idea is that fostering manufacturing growth through an export-oriented strategy will boost the demand for labor in related sectors. However, despite numerous studies demonstrating a positive relationship between trade liberalization and socioeconomic indicators, the impact of trade on gender equality, particularly concerning export performance, remains relatively unexplored. Our research underscores the need for a shift in this narrative, emphasizing the importance of trade policies that address gender equality in Indonesia. A foreign demand shock could yield gendered consequences through two primary channels. First, the shock may drive the adoption of new technologies, leading to the expansion of capital-intensive sectors. These sectors might necessitate fewer gender-specific skills, potentially increasing women’s participation in the labor market. Second, foreign demand may selectively target sectors with a higher concentration of female or male workers. For example, suppose foreign demand disproportionately affects female-dominant sectors. In that case, one might anticipate an increase in the wage level for women, consequently reducing the female-male wage gap in those sectors. At the household level, this shock could influence intrahousehold bargaining power for women, potentially resulting in more women choosing to participate in the labor market. Empirical evidence on the impact of trade liberalization on women’s employment in developing countries, primarily measured through tariff reduction, presents ambiguous results. In some instances, tariff reduction is associated with lower FLFP, as observed in Uganda (Giovannetti et al., 2022), Mexico (Saure & Zoabi, 2014), and Brazil (Gaddis & Pieters, 2017). Conversely, other studies have found that trade liberalization creates opportunities for women to enter the labor market, as seen in Egypt (Robertson et al., 2021), Turkey (Başlevent & Onaran, 2004), and China (Dai et al., 2021). The empirical evidence on welfare gains is also inconclusive. Some literature suggests that exposure to trade liberalization opens opportunities for women to participate in the formal economy (Conolly, 2022; Brussevich, 2018; Bussmann, 2009; Ben Yahmed & Bombarda, 2020). Regarding the wage gap, there is evidence indicating that trade liberalization helps women secure higher-paying jobs, thereby reducing the gender wage gap (Besedeš et al., 2021; Benguria & Ederington, 2023), but contradictory findings also exist (Juhn et al., 2014). Additionally, other studies highlight unintended consequences of trade liberalization, including reduced schooling (Atkin, 2016), increased deaths of despair (Pierce & Schott, 2020), lower fertility (Do et al., 2016), and heightened domestic violence (Erten & Keskin, 2021; Chong & Velásquez, 2024)

records.title: Trade openness and employment: Implications on urbanization in Sub-Saharan Africa
records.venue: International Journal of Management Research and Economics
records.abstract: Why are African countries urbanizing so fast?How do cities promote growth and why is it important to solve urban issues in Africa?In the context of higher push for trade liberalization multilaterally, it is not trivial to ask these set of question.In this study the main objective is to check the influence of trade openness of African economies on their urbanization rate.We also assess, how evolution of non-agricultural employment has also impacted this rate.We used panel data specifications, both in static and dynamic design.The data used are collected between 1990 and 2019 on 38 African countries.Although generally urbanization has increased during recent years in Africa, regions have experienced different pathways in the process.The results show that both trade openness and non-agricultural employment have been motivation for people to urbanize over years, in Africa.When we consider countries with high amount of people living in slums, they are more driven by employment purpose.Other variables such as per capita GDP and the fertility rate have positive and significant influence, while FDI and national investment have mixed impact.It is important to collaborate in a continental level to take advantage of the rapid urbanization.

records.abstract: This Technical Paper reports on a body of research conducted for the OECD Development Centre by Donald J. Robbins. It examines the patterns and determinants of rapidly rising educational attainment in six Latin American countries — Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Mexico and Uruguay — all of which illustrate the sweeping transformations in growth, demographics and education now occurring in much of the world. records.title: Contributions of agricultural economics to critical policy issues: selected papers presented at the XXVI IAAE conference
records.abstract: Agricultural economists are well aware of the many demands by policy makers and the wider society for improving the basic conditions of food security, poverty reduction, clean environment, and efficient, if not fair, trade. Traditional research issues related to production efficiency and technology adoption have, therefore, gradually been broadened to include several new topics in the research agenda, addressing questions of food safety, supply chain integration, water scarcity and biodiversity management, migration, and the nonfarm economy. The conference program for the 26th Conference of the International Association of Agricultural Economics (IAAE) provided a wide opportunity for scholars to present their research findings and to enter into debate with peers and policy makers. The conference took place in Gold Coast (Australia) and assembled more than 1,000 attendants during the week of 12–18 August 2006. The conference committee was extremely pleased to receive almost 850 contributed papers and after thorough review a total of 358 papers were selected, of which eventually 320 were presented in 72 panel sessions.1 A particular effort was made to structure the paper presentations along a number of thematic lines, thus enabling the participants to discuss related issues and compare the research methodologies applied to similar questions. Another important consideration was to define tracks throughout the program. Thus, six critical policy issues emerged as major areas of concern to researchers: Poverty and Food Security (41 papers), Markets and Institutions (70 papers), Technical Change in Agriculture (49 papers), Environment and Development (58 papers), Consumers and Supply Chains (57 papers), and Trade and Integration (46 papers). The first two issues focus on the prospects for reducing hunger and poverty, either through targeted support measures or by improving poor peoples' access to factor markets and institutions. The next two issues address different options for improving resource use efficiency and environmental sustainability in agricultural production. Finally, the last two issues deal with commodity markets and exchange, trade regulations, and the functioning of (inter)national value chains. We will discuss briefly the most important demands to the profession that are relevant in each of these policy areas, followed by an overview of recent contributions from research to address these issues. Main attention is given to the identification of new topics and/or innovative analytical approaches that were presented during the conference.2 The selected papers included in this special issue provide an adequate illustration of the progress in our professional field in each of the thematic fields and can thus be considered as outstanding pieces of research that deserve our full attention. Problems of (rural) poverty and food security have always received major attention in agricultural economics. The fundamental role of the agricultural sector in providing food to the growing urban population during the transition process of the economy, and the possibilities for improving agricultural productivity (per unit of land and labor) represent classical—albeit still highly relevant—research issues (Johnston and Mellor, 1961; Schultz, 1964; Timmer, 2002). Food security is increasingly addressed from the demand side, paying attention to rural employment and purchasing power as key determinants for getting access to food. Consequently, rural poverty should also be considered in relation to the imperfect functioning of factor and commodity markets and the prevailing constraints in the institutional setting (see also Section 3), thus giving rise to a more complete understanding of the structural causes of chronic poverty and food insecurity (Pingali, 2006). During the last decade, the discussion on rural poverty has been substantially broadened, paying attention to the options for nonfarm and off-farm employment and (inter)national migration as potential pathways out of poverty (Haggblade et al., 2002). The classical debate regarding the future of smallholder farms thus became more oriented toward so-called outside options (Lipton, 2005). Whereas the importance of labor market engagement is now generally acknowledged, it became also clear that this may give rise to large socioeconomic differentiation and new inequalities (Reardon et al., 1992). China is a critical case in this respect, facing rapidly increasing income gaps between rural and urban areas. Within the framework of the Millennium Development Goals, the attention for measuring progress in poverty reduction and for identifying pockets of chronic poverty strongly increased. The growing availability of detailed data sets for poverty measurement—made available from the country-wide Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers—encouraged new research regarding intertemporal poverty dynamics, spatial poverty targeting, and intrahousehold income distribution. In addition, innovative analytical tools for analyzing poverty-growth linkages at household, village, and regional level enable a better understanding of the diversity of pathways out of poverty. The three selected papers included in this special issue address poverty and food security from different angles. Arndt and Simler present a poverty analysis using endogenous absolute poverty lines with data from Mozambique, proposing a bootstrapping method for reducing the impact of sampling errors on poverty measures. They consistently demonstrate that this procedure, accounting for specified differences in poverty across geographical domains, has many advantages compared to traditional approaches. Yamano analyzes the long-term economic impacts of orphanhood mostly as a result of the AIDS epidemic, examining the education attainment and land inheritance of former orphans, who have lost at least one parent before reaching the age of 15 years, using household survey data from Kenya. The paper finds clear indications of lower educational attainment among former maternal orphans, but no significant difference in land inheritance. Finally, Kuiper and Ruben provide a stylized microsimulation model with material from a remote village in Northern Ethiopia to analyze the role of heterogeneous household assets in policies aiming at poverty reduction, indicating the implications for within-village income inequality and soil erosion. Three sets of policies are explored: technology improvement, infrastructure investment, and off-farm employment through migration or cash for work programs. While single policy instruments could reduce poverty headcount but frequently increase income inequality, combining market and employment policies assists poorer households better to overcome their asset limitations. Reducing the reliance of households on agriculture offers a win-win situation of reducing poverty and maintaining natural resources. Combining policies thus may be helpful to overcome asset limitations, to target policies to the poorest households and to reduce income inequalities. Market and institutional reforms are increasingly considered as a key element in policy strategies toward economic participation and sustainable growth. In many developing countries, structural adjustment programs (SAP) that started in the 1980s were intended to reduce market failures and to eliminate the traditional urban bias (Krueger, 1992). In a similar vein, reforms in property rights regimes (i.e., land titling) and privatization of former state services were meant to accompany a more market-based development. However, given the fact that rural markets in developing countries are rather thin and that barriers to entry tend to prevent real competition, results of the SAPs proved to be rather ambiguous (Badiane, 2000). Recent progress in thinking about the nature of rural markets and the endogenous character of agrarian institutions (Binswanger, 2006) gives room to new research concerning the role of transaction costs, risk management, and property rights regimes in economic development. Attention is therefore given to options for strengthening institutional relations and collective action between rural agents (including public–private partnerships) and strategies for managing price variability over time and space (Gilbert, 1998). Earlier analyses regarding the operations of factor markets for land, labor, and finance markets (Binswanger et al., 1994) are extended to adequately address market interlinkages, while strategies for improved commodity market integration and supply chain management are launched to improve price transmission and bargaining power (see also Section 6). The three selected papers that deal with rural markets and institutions provide a good illustration of current progress in research. The paper by Fort analyzes the impact of changes in asset inequality on economic growth, using a time-variant measure for land distribution with a panel database that includes observations for more than 30 countries over three decades. A system GMM estimator is used to generate unbiased and consistent regression estimates. The study finds robust and significant negative signs for land inequality in the growth regressions, indicating that changes in asset distribution are an important factor in economic development. Differences in property rights regimes and education prove to be critical to guarantee adequate transmission. Brosig et al. analyze the dynamics of labor market participation of Chinese rural households. Based on a farm household framework, the choice between four distinct labor market participation states is empirically analyzed. A discrete time hazard approach is used to analyze households' labor market participation histories, particularly the movements between autarky and participation and the shifts between part- and full-time farming. Results suggest a decreasing risk of moving from one regime to another with an increasing time a household resides in one of these states. Furthermore, the likelihood of starting any participation in labor markets and to start part-time farming are considerably higher than to end participation or to return to full-time farming. Kassie and Holden analyze the efficiency of sharecropping systems in Ethiopia, comparing the traditional model of the Marshallian inefficiency with threats of eviction hypotheses that have opposite effects on land productivity of sharecropped plots. Empirical results were consistent with the latter hypothesis, finding higher land productivity on sharecropped plots than on share tenants' own plots, and higher land productivity on sharecropped plots of nonkin than compared to kin tenants. The data analysis allows controls for unobservable household characteristics and for observable plot characteristics. First-order stochastic dominance analysis indicates that sharecropped plots' yield distribution clearly dominated the yield distribution from share tenants' own plots, whereas nonkin sharecropped plots' output value distribution also dominated the output value distribution from kin sharecrop plots. Research on improved and more efficient production technologies for cropping and livestock activities belongs to the core of the agricultural economics profession. Based on extensive field surveys among representative farmers, sound conclusions can be drawn regarding optimal input allocation and output mix under given market conditions (Ali and Byerlee, 1991; Battese, 1992). In addition, many research efforts have been devoted to a better understanding of adoption behavior, considering farm size, education, and market linkages as critical farm household characteristics (Feder et al., 1985). Finally, considerable evidence has been raised to establish the rate of returns to different types of investments in agricultural R&D (Alston et al., 1995) Analytical procedures for a sound analysis of technical change in agriculture are nowadays well established. Partial approaches have been replaced by whole-farm analysis, and frontier techniques are commonly used to identify the yield gap. In addition to mathematical programming methods, econometric and (non)parametric techniques are widely applied to detect underlying causes of yield differences (Coelli, 1995). Dynamic efficiency studies relying on panel data are increasingly used to decompose efficiency differences. New study areas related to issues of biotechnology adoption, integrated pest and nutrient management, and organic farming are addressed with similar techniques. The debate on the role of technology for agricultural and rural development has been gradually shifting in recent years, devoting more attention to (i) aspects of risk management as a key condition for smallholder adoption, (ii) the adaptation of farming systems to major climatic challenges (see Section 5), and (iii) the implications of market linkages for dovetailing farmers' production decisions to consumer demands (see Section 6). The conference papers selected for inclusion in this special issue provide adequate state-of-the-art research regarding the role of technology change. Börner et al. analyze the impact of rainfall and price variability on rangeland management decisions in the South African savanna region. Using stochastic and deterministic simulation models, their results indicate that price policies only have a limited impact for reducing bush encroachment, whereas better timing of animal sales and purchases would yield more pronounced utility effects. Also more effective technologies for fire control are promising measures to encourage sustainable rangeland management. The paper by Diagne and Demont takes a new look at empirical adoption models, providing a detailed analysis of the differences in technology adoption between a treatment and a control group, using propensity score matching to control for unobserved differences. Data from rice farmers in Cote d'Ivoire have been used to show that the potential adoption rates of new rice varieties might have been considerably larger if exposure to new technologies would have been offered to a larger population. The interface between development and environment has been subject to much research, originating through the well-known debates on the Kuznetz curve (Grossmann and Krueger, 1995). In subsequent periods, much attention has been devoted to microeconomic options for reducing environmental externalities, and macroeconomic policies for balancing production and environmental concerns. Recent studies are especially concerned with the management of limited water and energy resources and the remaining biodiversity at local and regional level, and with the implications of carbon and greenhouse gas emissions for climate change at global and local level. Agricultural policies for the environment are also considering new instruments, ranging from public taxation to payments for environmental services. While in Western countries options for rewarding multifunctional agriculture are introduced, in many developing countries (inter)national compensation payments still scarcely reach primary producers. The implementation of efficient and equitable regimes for water tariffs, biodiversity control, and carbon payments still meets numerous institutional constraints related to monitoring, enforcement, and control (Baland et al., 2007). Analytical methods for addressing environmental concerns in agricultural economics are developing rapidly. Starting with traditional cost-benefit analysis, most recent studies now apply some kind of integrated bioeconomic approach that accounts for feedback mechanisms. In addition, regional (watershed) models that include spatial distribution effects are increasingly used. A Two-Wheeled Type Vehicle to Carry Luggage in Cooperation with Human
records.abstract: In recent years, the decline in the total population due to aging and a declining birth rate has become a problem in Japan. It is a concern that the declining population will result in a serious labor shortage. For example, the labor shortage is increasing in freight forwarding and service industries. Automation is being promoted by introducing robots and the like. The purpose of research is the realization of an assisting vehicle using an inverted two-wheeled luggage-transport vehicle. Inverted two-wheeled vehicles have the advantages of high mobility, such as small size, cost, and the ability to turn on the spot. These reasons are advantages of a new assist vehicle. Since the type of vehicle is an unstable system, stabilization is necessary. Therefore, cooperative operation with humans is realized by inverted control and force control that introduces variable gain. The proposed control method is derived theoretically and its effectiveness is confirmed by experiments.

records.title: Parental Resources, Sibship Size, and Educational Performance in 20 Countries
records.abstract: We study whether having several siblings decreases the level of educational performance of adolescents and whether this phenomenon can be compensated by other factors such as the economic or cultural resources of the parents. Based on this compensation model, parental resources should be associated with children's educational attainments more strongly in families with a higher rather than a lower number of children. We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) data from 20 Western countries and found that better family wealth, an increased level of parental education, and a higher parental occupational status were associated with increased educational attainments more strongly among 15-year-old children who have siblings than among children without siblings. The same effect was not found in the case of family cultural possessions. Although parental resources may matter more in larger families than in smaller families, some types of resources are more important than others regarding compensation.

records.title: HIVAIDS and Fertility
records.abstract: This paper studies the response of fertility to the HIV/AIDS epidemic in sub-Saharan Africa. Standard models of fertility have ambiguous predictions in this context. Because childbirth requires unprotected sex (which increases the risk of contracting HIV), we might expect HIV/AIDS to reduce fertility through an infection avoidance motive. Adding to this decline, HIV infection may itself reduce fecundity among infected women. However, because HIV/AIDS affects the expected longevity of children, a quantity-quality model of childbearing would predict an increase in fertility. I use repeated cross-sections of the Demographic and Health Surveys for twelve countries in sub-Saharan Africa to examine this question empirically. Using individual birth histories from these data, I construct estimates of the regional total fertility rate over time. In a difference-in-differences approach, I compare regional HIV prevalence to changes in total fertility rates from the late 1980s to the present. My results suggest that HIV/AIDS had very little impact on fertility, both overall and in a sample of HIV-negative women.

records.title: What Explains Iran’s Low Female Labor Force Participation?
records.abstract: That women’s labor force participation in the Islamic Republic of Iran has been consistently low is well known, but explanations vary as to the principal causes. Moreover, many studies examine the female economically active population in aggregate, without sociodemographic distinctions. The puzzle is why women remain under-represented in Iran’s labor force despite high educational attainment, later marriage, smaller family size, and the country’s economic difficulties. Drawing on household surveys by the Statistical Center of Iran, we put the spotlight on the waged and salaried employment patterns of urban married women, who dominate the female labor force, and we compare patterns in two time periods: the economic growth period of 2005–2007 and the economic crisis period of 2017–2020. In examining the structural and institutional factors that explain women’s high unemployment and their tendency to drop out of the labor force following marriage and childbirth, we elucidate the roles of sanctions, economic cycles, declining government recruitment, discriminatory laws, and gendered wage gaps. We also highlight similarities and differences between Iran and other countries in the Middle East and North Africa.
